rows.t: Antique quadruple plate item marked "Union Met Works".

det.desc: Quadruple plate refers to a type of silver-plated metalware where the base metal is coated with four times the amount of silver typically used in standard silver plating. This process was popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, offering a more durable and luxurious finish than single or double plate, making it a more affordable alternative to solid silver. Items were often marked with terms like "Quadruple Plate" or "4x" to denote this higher quality plating. Union Metal Works was a manufacturer of silver-plated hollowware and flatware, operating primarily in the United States during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They produced a range of household items, from serving spoons and forks to pitchers and trays, often featuring intricate designs characteristic of the Victorian and Edwardian eras. Their "Quadruple Plate" items are recognized by collectors for their craftsmanship and historical significance as examples of mass-produced, yet elegant, tableware.

rows.t: Antique coat of Arms Black Metal "GUN POWDER" Cylinder Canister w lid

det.desc: This is a large antique japanned (black-lacquered) metal gunpowder storage/display canister featuring the coat of arms and motto of Belfast. Identification • The gold lettering reads “GUN POWDER.” • The central heraldic design is the official coat of arms of Belfast (granted/confirmed 1890, though elements are earlier): a shield with a ship on waves, a pile of vair, and a canton with a bell, flanked by a wolf (dexter) and seahorse (sinister), with the crest of a seahorse and the motto “PRO TANTO QUID RETRIBUAMUS” (“What return shall we make for so much?” / “For so much, what shall we repay?” — from Psalm 116). These large cylindrical tins were typically used in 19th- or early-20th-century gunsmiths’ or sporting-goods shops for bulk black powder storage or as counter/display canisters. The Belfast arms strongly suggest an Irish (Northern Irish) origin or retail connection. Condition (from the photo) Visible surface wear, scratches, scuffs, and some loss to the japanning and gilt decoration are present, which is typical for age. The lid appears intact and the overall form is good, with the arms and lettering still clearly legible.
